newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures remained rangebound on Friday as lingering concerns about how the new government will pay for its spending measures outlined on Thursday were offset by a belief the government will probably be cautious in 1997, the qualifying year for monetary union.
Traders said the session had been relatively quiet but a that there were plenty of buyers on dips, keeping the bond futures contract buoyed above 128.50, seen as a key level.
Analysts said it was too early to have a clear view of the measures presented by Prime Minister Lionel Jospin until the results of a public finance audit were unveiled in July.

They said that, although most feared the audit would show the 1997 public deficit would be around 3.5 percent without offsetting measures, the focus was likely to shift away from France until precise details were known and the government had presented its mini-budget after the summer break.

Some analysts said the net impact of the spending measures might not be that great, with savings from other areas - such as means testing family allowances - or the reduction of perks on savings vehicles such as life insurance products, acting as a counterbalance.
"I wasn't too concerned about the measures yesterday. It looks like they will be financed by redeployment of spending," Joanne Perez, strategist at Merrill Lynch said.
Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, said the audit in itself provided Jospin with some flexibility in implementing new spending measures, at least in 1997.
"He could use it to say the situation is more acute and serious than he thought, so things may not happen that quickly," Lindsay said.
"He won't break any promises he just may not fulfil them in such a timely fashion and in terms of the magic 1997 the longer he stalls the better for the Maastricht criteria," he said.

Stuart Thomson, economist at Credit Agricole Indosuez also thought the delay before introducing a mini-budget would buy the new government time to see what additional measures Germany might take to get its deficit to three percent of GDP. "The assumption being whatever Germany does France will match."
As result, they said the impact on the bond market would be fairly limited for now and domestic investors would be there to buy on dips, especially if 10-year yields neared 5.90 percent.

Lindsay said there could be scope for some outperformance at the front of the curve as the worst of the political uncertainty was out of the way, the franc had remained stable and there was little chance of interest rates being raised.
September PIBOR rose two basis points on Friday to 96.54 while the French franc retreated from an early low of 3.3767 against the mark to trade at 3.3745 at 1550 GMT.
